# Closing Recon-Dominator's Three Deepest Blind Spots

Recon-dominator's three weakest areas share a single underlying problem: each one currently trusts a signal that is trivially wrong in documented, real-world cases — a linked `<script>` tag that omits unlinked routes, a CNAME chain that misses an entire hijacking class, and a version string that silently lies about patch status. The highest-leverage fixes are not new attack classes but concrete, stdlib-only additions that close gaps the codebase has already half-anticipated: `cve_lookup.py` already defines `OSV_API` and `OSV_ECOSYSTEMS` constants and documents an `"osv-exact-match"` range tier in its own comments, yet no `lookup_via_osv()` function exists anywhere in the file — the single most-cited fix in this research (Anchore's production data shows swapping CPE matching for structured advisory data like OSV/GHSA cuts false positives by **up to 80%** with only 11 new false negatives) is scaffolded but never wired up ([Anchore](https://anchore.com/blog/say-goodbye-to-false-positives/)). Meanwhile `js_recon.py` already ports jsluice's AST-matcher logic into regex and recovers source maps without touching the VLQ-encoded `mappings` field, but never runs a secrets-regex pass over what it recovers — the exact step both of the two confirmed 2024-2026 bug-bounty writeups found in this research actually hinged on, including a **$25,000** bounty from Stripe keys sitting in a reconstructed source map exposing **$1.76 million** in live funds ([platformsecurity.com](https://platformsecurity.com/blog/little-bug-big-impact-25k-bounty)). And the subdomain pipeline's takeover check shells out to `dig` for CNAME chains only, which is structurally blind to "Sitting Ducks" NS-delegation hijacking — a technique 2024 research found exposed **over one million domains** and is explicitly characterized as "easier to perform, more likely to succeed, and harder to detect" than dangling-CNAME takeovers, precisely because it never touches a CNAME at all ([Krebs on Security](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2024/07/dont-let-your-domain-name-become-a-sitting-duck/)). What follows is the implementation-ready detection logic for each gap, with current codebase state called out explicitly so the next pass is additive, not a rewrite.

## Endpoint regex has one ancestor; the real frontier is what comes after the match

Every popular JS-mining tool in the open-source ecosystem traces back to **one regex**. LinkFinder's five-alternative pattern, written by Gerben Javado in 2017, is reused verbatim by GoLinkFinder and trimmed by two small deltas in JSFinder (which drops the extension-less REST-path branch and narrows one character class) — there is no meaningful competing lineage, just the same pattern re-hosted across Python and Go ([LinkFinder source](https://github.com/GerbenJavado/LinkFinder/blob/master/linkfinder.py), [JSFinder source](https://github.com/Threezh1/JSFinder/blob/master/JSFinder.py), [GoLinkFinder source](https://github.com/0xsha/GoLinkFinder/blob/master/GoLinkFinder.go)). `js_recon.py` already carries this exact pattern as `ENDPOINT_REGEX`, which is the right call — it uses only basic character classes and alternation with no backreferences, so it runs unmodified on raw minified text with no beautification step required. The newer generation abandoned regex outright: BishopFox's `jsluice` (the engine behind Katana's `-jsluice` mode) parses JS into a real tree-sitter syntax tree specifically because regex cannot disambiguate *which* call is a genuine `fetch`/`axios`/XHR invocation versus an unrelated quoted string ([jsluice url-matchers.go](https://github.com/BishopFox/jsluice/blob/main/url-matchers.go)). The practical payoff for a stdlib-only tool is that jsluice's matcher *logic* — not its parser — ports cleanly to regex for the common literal-argument case, and `js_recon.py`'s `FETCH_RE`, `AXIOS_METHOD_RE`, `JQUERY_RE`, and `XHR_OPEN_RE` already encode exactly jsluice's documented guard conditions, including the method-token check (`GET|HEAD|OPTIONS|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE`) that jsluice uses specifically to stop `window.open` from false-positiving as an XHR call ([jsluice url-match-xhr.go](https://github.com/BishopFox/jsluice/blob/main/url-match-xhr.go)). The ceiling is also already correctly acknowledged in the code's own comments: none of this can resolve a base URL built by concatenation (`BASE + "/users"`), a computed call target (`window["fetch"]`), or multi-statement URL construction — those require real AST parsing or JS execution, and the codebase explicitly skips rather than guesses at them, which is the right epistemic posture.

What the regex catches depends on `maybe_url()`, jsluice's last-resort string filter, ported line-for-line from its Go source and already present in `js_recon.py`:

```python
def maybe_url(s):
    if not any(c in s for c in "/?."):
        return False
    if any(c in s for c in " ()!<>'\"`{}^$,"):
        return False
    if s.startswith("/"):
        return True
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(s)
    if parsed.scheme and parsed.scheme.lower() not in ("http", "https"):
        return False
    host = parsed.hostname or ""
    if len(host.split(".")) > 1:
        return True
    if parsed.query:
        return True
    if "." not in parsed.path:
        return False
    ext = parsed.path.rsplit(".", 1)[-1]
    return ext in FILE_EXTENSIONS
```

This is the precision filter that keeps a broad `ENDPOINT_REGEX` sweep from drowning in noise, and it is exactly what jsluice itself falls back to after every structured matcher fails ([jsluice maybeurl.go](https://github.com/BishopFox/jsluice/blob/main/maybeurl.go)). One gap worth flagging: the current implementation never runs this filter as a standalone catch-all over *every* quoted string in a file — it only gates `ENDPOINT_REGEX` matches. A broad `r'''(['"\`])((?:\\.|(?!\1).)*?)\1'''` sweep piped through `maybe_url()` would additionally catch calls through renamed or wrapped request helpers (`const f = axios; f.get(...)`, `import {request as r} from "./api"`) that every call-name-specific regex, including jsluice's own structured matchers, will always miss.

Source-map recovery is the highest-value-per-line-of-code technique in this entire area, because it requires **zero decoding of the VLQ-encoded `mappings` field**. A source map is one JSON object (version, file, sources, sourcesContent, names, mappings — standardized as ECMA-426 since December 2024), and the `sources`/`sourcesContent` arrays alone disclose the entire original module and directory tree even when no text is recoverable ([ECMA-426](https://426.ecma-international.org/1.0/index.html)). `js_recon.py`'s `recover_sourcemap()` already does exactly this — find the `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment or fall back to the `.map` naming convention, then `json.loads()` the result and read `sources`/`sourcesContent` directly. This correctly matches both documented real cases: the $25,000 Stripe-key bounty (researcher used a tool called SourceMapper purely to reconstruct source text, no VLQ math) and the Apple App Store leak, where a researcher used a browser "Save All Resources" extension to recover complete Svelte/TypeScript source, state management, and routing configuration that was subsequently forked over **8,000 times** on GitHub before takedown ([escape.tech](https://escape.tech/blog/apple-app-store-source-map-leak/)). Escape's own scanning telemetry found this exposure class — a live JS file referencing a fetchable, unauthenticated `.map` — in **70% of the organizations it scanned** (vendor's own customer base, not an industry-wide sample, but still a signal this is default-assume-present, not an edge case) ([escape.tech](https://escape.tech/blog/apple-app-store-source-map-leak/)). The concrete gap: `js_recon.py` stores recovered `sourcesContent` in `sourcemap_hits` but never scans it. Both confirmed cases found their secrets through *manual* reading specifically because the hardcoded keys had no naming pattern automated secret-scanners would flag — which argues for piping every recovered source file through a SecretFinder-style regex dictionary before anything else, since that is the step that turned "disclosed source" into "disclosed credentials" in both cited incidents:

```python
SECRET_PATTERNS = {
    "stripe_live_key": r"sk_live_[0-9a-zA-Z]{24}",
    "aws_access_key_id": r"A[SK]IA[0-9A-Z]{16}",
    "google_api_key": r"AIza[0-9A-Za-z-_]{35}",
    "json_web_token": r"ey[A-Za-z0-9-_=]+\.[A-Za-z0-9-_=]+\.?[A-Za-z0-9-_.+/=]*",
    "generic_bearer": r"bearer [a-zA-Z0-9_\-\.=:_\+\/]{5,100}",
    "possible_hardcoded_cred": r"(?i)(password|pwd|passwd|secret)\s*[`=:\"]+\s*[^\s,;)]{4,}",
}
# Run against every recovered sourcesContent string AND every raw js_text
# chunk already fetched -- this closes the one concrete step both the
# $25k and Apple writeups actually depended on, which recover_sourcemap()
# currently stops one step short of.
```

Build manifests are the cleanest "hidden route" signal of the three bundler ecosystems, and here the asymmetry across bundlers is sharp enough to matter operationally. Next.js exposes `self.__BUILD_MANIFEST` at `_next/static/<buildId>/_buildManifest.js`, mapping every known client-side route to its required chunks regardless of whether anything on the rendered page links to it — `js_recon.py`'s `fetch_next_build_manifest()` already extracts the `buildId` from either the HTML or the manifest path and strips the JS-literal wrapper before `json.loads()`. Vite's `.vite/manifest.json` is stricter JSON needing no stripping at all, and its `dynamicImports` array is close to a direct route list because dynamic imports are how SPA code-splitting is implemented in practice ([Vite backend integration guide](https://vite.dev/guide/backend-integration)) — `fetch_vite_manifest()` already reads this correctly. Plain webpack is the deliberate gap in both the research and the current code: there is no single stable global name for webpack's JSONP chunk-registration array across versions and configs, so full runtime enumeration without executing the bundle is a best-effort approximation, not a guarantee — a limitation corroborated by Rspack's own documentation of its webpack-compatible `'array-push'` JSONP chunk-loading format and by the existence of a dedicated `chunk-manifest-webpack-plugin` built specifically to export a chunk-id-to-asset map as a separate static file, which implies that mapping is not reliably readable from the runtime chunk by default. `js_recon.py`'s `CHUNK_HINT_RE`/`HASHED_ASSET_RE` catch-all (crawling path-based and content-hashed filenames referenced from within already-fetched JS) is the correct bundler-agnostic baseline, but it does not yet attempt the webpack-specific chunk-id-to-hash object literal that the runtime/entry chunk commonly embeds for its own filename resolution:

```python
CHUNKMAP_RE = re.compile(r'\{\s*(?:\d+\s*:\s*"[a-f0-9]+"\s*,?\s*)+\}')

def extract_chunk_hash_map(runtime_js):
    m = CHUNKMAP_RE.search(runtime_js)
    if not m:
        return {}
    quoted = re.sub(r'(?<=[{,])\s*(\d+)\s*:', r'"\1":', m.group(0))
    return json.loads(quoted)  # {chunk_id: hash} -- heuristic, not guaranteed-complete
```

This is explicitly the "a real JS engine would be needed to be fully correct" case — custom `chunkFilename` templates or non-default `publicPath` computation will defeat it — but it is a strict addition on top of the existing catch-all, not a replacement, and costs nothing when it fails to match. One confirmed documentation gap worth carrying into any writeup of this feature: the `__BUILD_MANIFEST` mechanism is tooled and documented primarily around Next.js's older Pages Router, and App Router's server-reference/action manifest equivalent was not confirmed in this research pass.

## DNSSEC zone-walking still works, until live signing shows up

NSEC zone-walking is not a theoretical attack — it is a fully solved, linear-time technique against any zone signed with plain NSEC, and plain NSEC is **56% of all signed zones** in a 2024 Tranco Top-1M measurement (versus 42% for NSEC3) ([arXiv 2403.15233](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.15233)). The mechanism is a DNSSEC-OK query for a name that does not exist; the NXDOMAIN response's AUTHORITY section carries an NSEC record whose "next domain name" field proves no name exists between the queried name and that next one — which simultaneously hands over the next name to query, walking the entire zone in canonical order until the chain wraps back to the start ([APNIC](https://blog.apnic.net/2023/01/17/subdomain-enumeration-with-dnssec)). A separate DNS-abuse technical report found roughly **2.4 million** correctly-signed second-level domains publishing plain, directly-walkable NSEC records ([arXiv 2212.08879](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.08879)). NSEC3 (RFC 5155) breaks plaintext walking by hashing owner names with SHA-1 before chaining them, but APNIC's own conclusion is blunt: "NSEC3 makes enumeration harder but doesn't prevent it" — many queries still harvest next-owner hashes (approximating zone size even with zero names recovered), and harvested hashes are crackable offline against a dictionary, just not via reusable rainbow tables, since the zone name itself feeds the hash ([APNIC](https://blog.apnic.net/2023/01/17/subdomain-enumeration-with-dnssec)). RFC 9276 confirms that additional iterations and salts add diminishing or no meaningful protection against this offline attack, and SHA-1 remains the only NSEC3 hash algorithm in real-world use — existing cracking tooling (`unhash`/`nsec3walker`, hashcat mode 8300, a John the Ripper jumbo patch from the `n3map` project) already targets exactly this.

Because Python's `socket` module only exposes `getaddrinfo`/`gethostbyname` — OS-resolver A/AAAA lookups with no ability to request NSEC/NSEC3 record types or set the DNSSEC-OK bit — a zero-dependency implementation has to build and parse raw DNS packets by hand over UDP/53, with an EDNS0 OPT pseudo-record carrying the DO bit set:

```python
import socket, struct

def build_nsec_query(qname, qtype=47):  # 47 = NSEC; use ANY to probe broadly
    header = struct.pack('>HHHHHH', 0x1337, 0x0000, 1, 0, 0, 1)
    labels = b"".join(bytes([len(l)]) + l.encode() for l in qname.rstrip(".").split(".")) + b"\x00"
    question = labels + struct.pack('>HH', qtype, 1)  # QCLASS=IN
    # EDNS0 OPT RR in the additional section, DO bit = high bit of the
    # repurposed TTL field -- mandatory, or no RRSIG/NSEC/NSEC3 comes back
    opt = b"\x00" + struct.pack('>HH', 41, 4096) + struct.pack('>BBH', 0, 0, 0x8000) + struct.pack('>H', 0)
    return header + question + opt

def walk_nsec(resolver_ip, zone_apex, max_hops=5000):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sock.settimeout(5)
    seen, current = set(), zone_apex
    while current not in seen and len(seen) < max_hops:
        seen.add(current)
        sock.sendto(build_nsec_query(current), (resolver_ip, 53))
        resp, _ = sock.recvfrom(4096)
        next_name = parse_nsec_next_name(resp)  # decode NSEC RDATA's uncompressed next-name field
        if not next_name or next_name == zone_apex:
            break
        current = next_name
    return sorted(seen)
```

The NSEC3 offline-cracking side needs only `hashlib`/`base64` beyond this, since the iterated hash is fully specified: `digest = sha1(wire_name + salt)`, repeated `iterations` more times, then encoded with Extended-Hex Base32 and compared against harvested next-hashed-owner values from the NSEC3 RDATA. The single most important operational caveat is that a growing share of the *most valuable* real-world targets are categorically immune to both techniques for a structural reason, not a cryptographic one: Cloudflare — one of the largest DNSSEC-signing providers on the internet — now live-signs denial-of-existence responses under what is standardized as **Compact Denial of Existence** (formerly "black lies"), synthesizing a single NSEC record directly on the queried nonexistent name itself, with no precomputed chain to walk at all ([draft-valsorda-dnsop-black-lies](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-valsorda-dnsop-black-lies); confirmed as the current standardization name at the [IETF 119 hackathon](https://www.bortzmeyer.org/hackathon-ietf-119.html)). This means a successful NSEC/NSEC3 harvest is itself a usable signal — it tells the operator the zone is *not* behind a major live-signing DNS provider, which narrows where to spend the rest of the enumeration budget. Whether AWS Route 53, Google Cloud DNS, or Akamai use an equivalent live-signing scheme was not confirmed in this research and should not be assumed either way.

Structurally distinct from anything DNSSEC-related is **"Sitting Ducks,"** the 2024 Infoblox/Eclypsium-documented domain-hijacking technique that exploits NS delegation rather than CNAME records. It targets domains whose DNS is delegated to a different authoritative provider than the registrar, where that delegation is additionally "lame" — the named nameservers lack the zone data to actually answer for it — letting an attacker claim the zone at the hosting provider without ever touching the victim's registrar or DNS-provider account ([Krebs on Security](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2024/07/dont-let-your-domain-name-become-a-sitting-duck/)). Industry reporting puts the exposure precondition at **over one million domains**, with one outlet separately reporting roughly **70,000 of approximately 800,000** assessed-vulnerable domains already hijacked by more than a dozen Russian-affiliated threat actors — these are two different metrics (exposure precondition versus confirmed hijacks) from different outlets, and the discrepancy is noted rather than resolved here ([SecurityAffairs](https://securityaffairs.com/166445/hacking/sitting-ducks-attack-technique.html); [TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2024/08/over-1-million-domains-at-risk-of.html)). Researchers explicitly describe it as "easier to perform, more likely to succeed, and harder to detect" than dangling-CNAME takeovers. This matters directly for recon-dominator's pipeline: `skills/cloud-pivot-finder/scripts/takeover_scanner.py` resolves CNAME chains (by shelling out to `dig`) and checks each target against a provider-fingerprint dictionary of NXDOMAIN/error strings — a well-built version of the standard technique, but one that is mechanistically incapable of ever finding a Sitting-Ducks-class hijack, no matter how complete its fingerprint database gets, because the vulnerable condition never touches a CNAME. The complementary, zero-overlap check is an NS-health probe using the same raw-UDP-DNS machinery built for NSEC walking above: resolve each (sub)domain's NS records, then query each listed nameserver directly for that zone's SOA, and flag REFUSED/SERVFAIL/timeout/non-authoritative responses as lame-delegation candidates. Yahoo's open-source Subdomain Sleuth already implements exactly this class of check against BIND zone files as a reference implementation ([awesome.ecosyste.ms listing](https://awesome.ecosyste.ms/)), and a University of Amsterdam student research project found 862 domains with lame NS delegations in its sample — a useful illustration of base rate, though a single unreviewed student project, not a population-level statistic ([rp.os3.nl](https://rp.os3.nl/2020-2021/p59/report.pdf)).

## Cloud naming conventions turn the subdomain list itself into the best wordlist

The strongest single data point in this research area is quietly simple: Fortinet's analysis of real-world S3 bucket-name trends found **28% of discovered bucket names were also valid, fully-qualified domain names** ([Fortinet](https://www.fortinet.com/resources/articles/trends-in-s3-targeting)). That statistic reframes the whole technique. The useful move is not "guess generic bucket names" — it is "take the subdomain list recon-dominator has already built, passively and actively, and replay every entry as a candidate cloud-resource name," because organizations overwhelmingly name cloud assets after domains they already control. Each major provider ties a predictable, DNS-visible hostname to an account or service name in a structurally different way, which changes how confidently a hit should be trusted:

| Provider / service | Naming pattern | Confidence of a hit | Key source |
|---|---|---|---|
| AWS S3 | `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com` (virtual-hosted) or path-style | High — direct asset | [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.eu/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/bucketnamingrules.html) |
| Azure Blob Storage | `{account}.blob.core.windows.net/{container}` | High — direct asset | [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/storageservices/naming-and-referencing-containers--blobs--and-metadata) |
| GCP Cloud Storage | Domain-named buckets supported directly (e.g. `static.example.com`) | High — direct asset | [Google Cloud docs](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/domain-name-verification) |
| Azure App Service | Legacy `<app>.azurewebsites.net`, globally predictable | Lower — predictable but not proof of a live, distinct app | [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/reference-dangling-subdomain-prevention?tabs=cli) |
| GCP Cloud Run | `SERVICE-PROJECTNUMBER.REGION.run.app`, fixed default URL | Lower — structured, extra guessable components | Google Cloud Run docs |
| GCP App Engine | `PROJECT_ID.REGION_ID.r.appspot.com`, with "soft routing" to the default service for nonexistent names | Low — a 200-OK can be a misleading soft-route, not a distinct asset | [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/google-app-engine-feature-abused-to-create-unlimited-phishing-pages/amp/) |
| CloudFront | Unique `*.cloudfront.net` per distribution, but routes by Host header, not by which hostname was dialed | Flag separately — hijack-adjacent, not a classic dangling-CNAME case | [Dark Reading](https://darkreading.com/cloud-security/don-t-call-aws-cloudfront-hijacking-problem-a-vulnerability) |

The App Engine "soft routing" behavior deserves its own callout: a request naming a nonexistent service, version, or instance under a valid project is still routed to that project's default service rather than 404ing, which means huge numbers of plausible-looking subdomain permutations under one project all resolve successfully with a valid Google-issued TLS certificate — a behavior BleepingComputer documents as actively abused in the wild to host phishing pages that evade naive indicator-of-compromise blocking. That makes a bare "resolves with 200-OK" check actively misleading for App Engine/Cloud Run-style compute hosts in a way it is not for storage buckets, so these two categories need different confidence tiers in any output the tool produces, not a single pass/fail. CloudFront's behavior is a second distinct trap: because routing is governed purely by the HTTP Host header rather than which `*.cloudfront.net` hostname was actually dialed, AWS's own `ListConflictingAliases` API exists specifically to let an operator find every other CNAME across the service overlapping a given one — and the `cloudfrunt` tool automates finding misconfigured distributions exploitable this way ([Dark Reading](https://darkreading.com/cloud-security/don-t-call-aws-cloudfront-hijacking-problem-a-vulnerability)). The implementable version of all of this is a short probe loop fed by the pipeline's own `subdomains.json` rather than a generic wordlist:

```python
CLOUD_SUFFIXES = {
    "s3": "{name}.s3.amazonaws.com",
    "azure_blob": "{name}.blob.core.windows.net",
    "gcs": "{name}.storage.googleapis.com",
    "azure_app": "{name}.azurewebsites.net",
    "cloud_run": None,  # needs project-number guessing, not a bare name
    "appengine": None,  # soft-routing makes a bare resolve check unreliable
}

def cloud_candidates_from_subdomains(subdomain_names):
    # subdomain_names: bare labels already discovered by passive/active recon,
    # e.g. "assets" from "assets.example.com" -- the candidate dictionary IS
    # the target's own enumerated names, not a generic bucket wordlist.
    candidates = []
    for name in subdomain_names:
        for provider, pattern in CLOUD_SUFFIXES.items():
            if pattern:
                candidates.append((provider, pattern.format(name=name)))
    return candidates
```

Certificate-transparency pivoting beyond substring search is the cheapest addition in this section, because recon-dominator already queries crt.sh per the existing SKILL.md pipeline. The documented technique is to pivot off a found certificate's issuer-populated Organization ("O=") field rather than just the domain name, surfacing sibling certificates, subsidiaries, or rebrands that a plain domain-substring query on crt.sh would never return ([SANS ISC Diary](https://isc.sans.edu/diary/24114)). This is a free second query against infrastructure the pipeline already calls. Three further active-pivoting techniques round out this area, all free of paid API keys: TLS-SAN extraction scoped to an entire IP range or ASN (`tlsx`-style), which surfaces hosts DNS enumeration alone misses entirely because it fingerprints infrastructure, not domain names ([ProjectDiscovery](https://blog.projectdiscovery.io/a-hackers-guide-to-ssl-certificates-featuring-tlsx/)); favicon-hash pivoting via a 32-bit MurmurHash3 of the favicon file matched against Shodan's `http.favicon.hash:` filter, with the explicit caveat that generic framework favicons (default Spring Boot's hash is a commonly cited example) produce false-positive matches that must be filtered before trusting a result ([infosecwriteups](https://infosecwriteups.com/how-to-find-subdomains-using-shodan-and-the-favicon-hash-trick-ac01741b0fb5)); and ASN-based reverse-PTR sweeps across an organization's confirmed-owned IP ranges (via bgp.he.net), which surface hostnames that never appear in any certificate or CT log at all, such as internal tools and mail infrastructure. None of this — DNSSEC walking, Sitting-Ducks NS-health checks, cloud-naming pivots, favicon hashing, or Organization-field CT pivoting — currently exists anywhere in the skills tree; a direct search across every script in the repository for DNSSEC/NSEC, favicon-hash, or cloud-storage-suffix logic returns nothing, confirming this is genuinely greenfield work for recon-dominator rather than a refinement of something partially built.

## Version strings lie three distinct ways, and the codebase has already fixed one of them

`cve_lookup.py`'s own development history is a useful map of this problem, because two of the three failure modes documented in the research are already fixed in committed code, and the third is scaffolded but dead. Backport patches that don't bump the version string are the best-documented failure mode industry-wide: Red Hat states plainly that it "usually does not rebase packages to entirely new versions" and instead backports fixes, citing CVE-2022-24070 as a worked example where Subversion 1.10 carried a backported fix that only Red Hat's RPM *release* suffix (not the version field) actually signals ([Red Hat](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/assessing-red-hat-ansible-automation-platform-vulnerabilities)). Debian's own Security FAQ recommends comparing the exact version against its advisories or running `apt-get changelog` ([Debian](https://www.debian.org/security/faq.html)), and the regreSSHion case (CVE-2024-6387) is a concrete, current instance where a Debian OpenSSH banner reading `9.2p1 Debian-2+deb12u3` was wrongly flagged by at least one checker because the fix lived entirely in the distro suffix, invisible to upstream version comparison ([happyDomain commit](https://git.nemunai.re/happyDomain/checker-ssh/commit/fb2ae7d9037ae4934714ec952c330935e40a1ffa)). Tenable runs dedicated "Backported Security Patch Detection" plugins and maintains a `backport.inc` code path specifically to suppress this noise ([Tenable plugin 39519](https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/39519)). `cve_lookup.py` already implements the stdlib-only version of this exact mitigation: a `_BACKPORT_SUFFIX_RE` pattern matching Debian/Ubuntu (`+deb12u3`-style) and RHEL/Fedora (`-1.el9`-style) suffixes, feeding a `_looks_backported()` check that sets a `backport_suspected` flag independent of the range-match verdict (lines 76-97 and 393-399 of the current file). This is a closed gap, not an open one — the honest remaining limitation, also stated in the code's own comments, is that stdlib Python with no shell or package-manager access cannot itself run `apt-get changelog` or query an OVAL feed, so the flag is correctly scoped as a confidence annotation for a human to verify, not a resolution.

Fork and rebrand false positives are the second mode, and here the WordPress ecosystem supplies unusually concrete documented incidents: a plugin developer confirmed in a WordPress.org support thread that their plugin was undiscoverable in Wordfence's database specifically because it "is indeed an early fork... [that had] become substantially different" ([WordPress.org support thread](https://remarpro.com/support/topic/vulnerability-reported-for-a-plugin-but-link-is-404-and-the-plugin-is-not-in-db)), and separately, Plugin Vulnerabilities documented Wordfence linking a fix to a plugin version that was never released at all, alongside a broader claim that WPScan's database "often" just copies another source's data and that Patchstack's data is "largely the same inaccurate data as Wordfence's" ([pluginvulnerabilities.com](https://www.pluginvulnerabilities.com/2024/01/22/many-cve-records-are-listing-the-wrong-versions-of-software-as-being-affected/)). This means cross-referencing multiple WordPress vulnerability-intelligence vendors does not reliably escape the problem, because they are not independent of each other. The clearest real instance of a fork being swapped in at the distribution level is Automattic forking WP Engine's "Advanced Custom Fields" into "Secure Custom Fields" and substituting it directly in the WordPress.org repository, migrating auto-update sites onto a completely different codebase under the hood ([WP Tavern](https://wptavern.com/acf-plugin-forked-to-secure-custom-fields-plugin)). `cve_lookup.py`'s `_matches_component()` already defends against the generic version of this with exact CPE product-name equality rather than substring containment — its own comments cite a real, previously-live bug where CVE-2026-28192 ("Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Upload in Piotnet Addons For Elementor Pro") was false-positiving as a match against core Elementor Pro, because substring matching cannot tell "Elementor Pro" apart from "Piotnet Addons For Elementor Pro." The current code (lines 296-313) now explicitly filters out addon-naming patterns ("for " preceding the product name) and fork-naming patterns (the product name followed by "fork," "clone," "alternative to," or "rebrand(ed)"). What remains open, and is explicitly labeled as such in the code's own `"keyword-only-unverified"` range-source tier, is the case where nothing structured or textual exists to confirm *or* refute a hypothesis — and the false-negative direction (a fork that genuinely is vulnerable but whose name diverges enough to escape the keyword gate entirely) has no documented real-world incident in this research at all; it is a logical implication of the same name-matching mechanism, not a confirmed gap, and should be reported to stakeholders with that distinction intact.

The third mode — coverage gaps for non-CPE ecosystems — is where the codebase shows the clearest sign of unfinished work. JFrog's contextual-analysis research, run against the ten most frequently reported CVEs across the two hundred most popular "latest"-tag Docker Hub images, found **78% of those CVE occurrences were "non-applicable"** once actual code-reachability was checked — meaning the bare "vulnerable version string present" signal was wrong roughly four times out of five in that sample ([InfoWorld/JFrog](https://www.infoworld.com/article/3677550/most-reported-cves-for-docker-hub-images-are-harmless.html)). Anchore's production telemetry is the more directly actionable number: moving supported ecosystems from NVD's CPE-string matching to GitHub Security Advisory data cut false positives by **2,000+** matches in their test set, up to an **80% reduction** for some ecosystems, at a cost of only 11 new false negatives — and Anchore Enterprise now disables CPE matching by default for every GHSA-covered ecosystem as a result ([Anchore](https://anchore.com/blog/say-goodbye-to-false-positives/)). This is not a data-absence problem — a VulCPE preprint reports that **93.55%** of NVD entries carry at least one valid CPE string — it is a matching-*precision* problem specific to CPE as an identifier scheme ([VulCPE, arXiv:2505.13895](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.13895v1)), reinforced by NIST's own abandoned attempt (NISTIR 8085) to derive better identifiers from SWID tags, a draft industry commentary says has been superseded by PURL (package URL) adoption instead ([Endor Labs](https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/whats-in-a-name-a-look-at-the-software-identification-ecosystem)). `cve_lookup.py` has clearly been written with this fix in mind and then stopped short of finishing it: `OSV_API = "https://api.osv.dev/v1/query"` and `OSV_ECOSYSTEMS = ["npm", "PyPI", "Go", "Maven", "crates.io", "RubyGems", "Packagist", "NuGet"]` are both defined near the top of the file, a comment references a `lookup_component_auto()` function, and the `range_source` field's own inline documentation lists `"osv-exact-match"` as a value "set only by `lookup_via_osv()`" — but neither `lookup_via_osv()` nor `lookup_component_auto()` is defined or called anywhere in the 509-line file, confirmed directly by searching the file. This is the single most surgical, lowest-risk fix available in this entire research pass: the integration point, naming, and even the output schema are already designed; what is missing is the function body itself — a plain stdlib HTTPS POST to OSV.dev's free, keyless API with the discovered package name/version/ecosystem, preferring its `affected[].ranges` data over NVD's CPE match whenever a component's `kind` indicates a language-ecosystem package rather than a CMS plugin.

Two supplementary, lower-confidence signals round out this area without needing new infrastructure. Patchstack's Threat Intelligence API models a genuinely richer schema than a single NVD CPE range — each record carries `affected_in`, `fixed_in`, and a `patched_in_ranges` array expressing different fix points across multiple active release branches, leaving `fixed_in` explicitly blank when no official patch exists rather than guessing ([Patchstack](https://docs.patchstack.com/api-solutions/threat-intelligence-api/api-properties/)) — useful as a CMS-specific analog to OSV/GHSA, with the same cross-vendor data-quality caveat raised above. And `api.wordpress.org`'s plugin-info endpoint exposes a `last_updated` timestamp that, cross-referenced against a CVE's disclosure date, is a directionally sound but unvalidated heuristic — strong in one direction only ("not updated since before disclosure" is a solid signal of "still vulnerable"), weak in the other, and documented as having its own history of stale or incorrect dates and caching lag ([WordPress.org support thread](https://wordpress.org/support/topic/api-wordpress-org-plugins-info-1-0-slug-json-returns-incorrect-version/)). Neither of these is implemented in the current code, and neither should replace the OSV integration — they are smaller, CMS-specific supplements to it.

## Conclusion

The pattern across all three areas is the same: the deepest, most current (2024-2026) techniques are not exotic — NSEC walking is a 2023-documented, linear-time attack; Sitting Ducks is a 2024 finding with a four-digit domain-count estimate; OSV-over-CPE is Anchore's shipped production default — but they are each invisible to a tool that only checks the thing it already knows how to check. A CNAME-only takeover scanner cannot find a lame delegation no matter how good its fingerprint list is; a CPE-only CVE matcher cannot find an npm advisory no matter how exact its product-name equality gets; an endpoint regex cannot find a secret it never scans for, no matter how faithfully it reproduces jsluice's matcher logic. The actionable implication is that the next engineering pass on recon-dominator should prioritize finishing what is already half-built — the `lookup_via_osv()` stub and a secrets-regex pass over recovered source maps are both smaller, lower-risk changes than anything else in this report and each map to one of the two best-evidenced statistics in the entire research set (Anchore's 80% false-positive reduction and the two confirmed source-map bounty cases) — before adding the genuinely greenfield work of DNS-protocol-layer probing and cloud-naming pivots, none of which exist anywhere in the pipeline today. The weakest evidentiary ground across all three areas is consistently the false-negative direction: no source in this research documents a real case of a fork evading CVE detection, a webpack chunk map being fully reverse-engineered without executing the bundle, or an independent, vendor-neutral measurement of bare version-range-comparison accuracy on its own — every hard number available comes from a vendor measuring the improvement of its own competing product, which should temper confidence in the exact percentages even while the direction of every finding points the same way.
